title: 1 Chronicles 16:37–43
context: 1 Chronicles 16:37–43 describes the arrangements David made after the ark came to Jerusalem. Asaph and his brothers minister continually before the ark in Jerusalem, while Zadok and his fellow priests serve before the LORD’s tabernacle at the high place at Gibeon, offering the daily burnt offerings according to the law (compare Exodus 29:38–42; Numbers 28:3–4). Chronicles later says the Tent of Meeting made by Moses was at Gibeon while the ark was in the tent David pitched in Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 1:3–4). The section names Heman and Jeduthun among the musicians and Obed-Edom among the doorkeepers; whether the Obed-Edom of 16:38 is one man or two, and how he relates to Obed-Edom the Gittite (13:13), is debated, and the count of sixty-eight relatives here differs from the sixty-two of Obed-Edom in the later list at 26:8. The closing verse parallels 2 Samuel 6:19b–20a; Chronicles does not include the exchange with Michal that follows there. Both traditions read the section as shared ground: worship is ordered, continual, and grounded in the LORD’s enduring loving kindness.

verses.text: So he left Asaph and his brothers there before the ark of the LORD’s covenant, to minister before the ark continually, as every day’s work required;
verses.arminianNotes:
David leaves Asaph and his brothers before the ark of the LORD’s covenant to minister continually, as each day’s work requires. Worship before the ark becomes a daily service.

Arminian readers see faithfulness expressed in daily, ordinary service, and they note that devotion to God is meant to be sustained in regular practice and not only in occasions of great celebration.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the continual ministry before the ark reflects God’s ordering of worship through appointed servants, and they see the daily pattern as a sign that God’s presence among his people is to be honored without interruption.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about steady and faithful worship.

verses.text: and Obed-Edom with their sixty-eight relatives; Obed-Edom also the son of Jeduthun and Hosah to be doorkeepers;
verses.arminianNotes:
Obed-Edom is appointed with sixty-eight relatives, and Obed-Edom the son of Jeduthun and Hosah are doorkeepers. Whether this verse speaks of one Obed-Edom or two is debated, and the later list counts sixty-two of Obed-Edom (26:8).

Arminian readers see a household once blessed by the ark’s presence now serving it, if the identification holds.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hold the identifications loosely, as the notes on 2 Samuel 6:10 do, and they read the verse as part of Chronicles’ careful record of those who guarded and served the ark.

Both traditions treat the numbers and identifications as matters for careful study rather than doctrine, and they record the differences without harmonizing them.

verses.text: and Zadok the priest and his brothers the priests, before the LORD’s tabernacle in the high place that was at Gibeon,
verses.arminianNotes:
Zadok the priest and his brothers the priests serve before the LORD’s tabernacle in the high place at Gibeon. Chronicles later says the Tent of Meeting made by Moses was there (2 Chronicles 1:3).

Arminian readers see two centers of worship in this period, the ark in Jerusalem and the tabernacle at Gibeon, and they note that faithful service continues in both places.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the distinction between the tent David pitched and the tabernacle at Gibeon helps explain why the altar service continued at Gibeon, and they see God’s ordinances maintained during a transitional period before the temple.

Both traditions read the verse as historical description and treat it as shared ground.

verses.text: to offer burnt offerings to the LORD on the altar of burnt offering continually morning and evening, even according to all that is written in the LORD’s law, which he commanded to Israel;
verses.arminianNotes:
At Gibeon the priests offer burnt offerings on the altar of burnt offering continually, morning and evening, according to all that is written in the LORD’s law. The daily offerings follow the law (Exodus 29:38–42; Numbers 28:3–4).

Arminian readers see the people’s faithful obedience to God’s revealed pattern of worship.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the phrase about all that is written in the LORD’s law, noting that the authority for the daily offerings is God’s written word, which matches the lesson of 15:13 and 15:15 about seeking God according to his ordinance.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about worship shaped by Scripture and offered faithfully every day.

verses.text: and with them Heman and Jeduthun and the rest who were chosen, who were mentioned by name, to give thanks to the LORD, because his loving kindness endures forever;
verses.arminianNotes:
With them are Heman and Jeduthun and others chosen by name to give thanks to the LORD, “because his loving kindness endures forever” Jeduthun appears where Ethan appeared in 15:17–19, and some interpreters identify the two, though this is debated.

Arminian readers see thanksgiving offered in response to God’s enduring love.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the refrain from 16:34 now becomes the stated purpose of appointed musicians, and that the verse uses the word chosen of those selected for this service, which concerns their office and is not a statement about salvation.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about thanksgiving grounded in God’s loving kindness.

verses.text: and with them Heman and Jeduthun with trumpets and cymbals for those that should sound aloud, and with instruments for the songs of God, and the sons of Jeduthun to be at the gate.
verses.arminianNotes:
Heman and Jeduthun have trumpets and cymbals for those who sound aloud, and instruments for the songs of God, and the sons of Jeduthun are at the gate. The musicians and gatekeepers each have their place.

Arminian readers see a variety of gifts and roles contributing to the worship of God, and they note that every role, whether music or guarding the gate, is a real service to the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the songs are called the songs of God, which they see as an indication that worship belongs to God and is shaped by his appointment rather than by human preference alone.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about ordered and joyful worship in which different servants each have their part.

verses.text: All the people departed, each man to his house; and David returned to bless his house.
verses.arminianNotes:
All the people depart, each to his house, and David returns to bless his house. The parallel is 2 Samuel 6:19b–20a, where the exchange with Michal follows; Chronicles does not include that exchange and moves on to chapter 17.

Arminian readers see the king carrying the blessing of the day into his own household, a picture of worship that shapes ordinary life.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the account ends in blessing, and that Chronicles’ arrangement leads directly to David’s desire to build a house for the LORD and God’s promise to build David’s house in chapter 17.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and avoid speculating about what Chronicles chose not to retell.
